newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistanis respond to Sharif's debt payment scheme.
newsitem.headline: Pakistanis respond to Sharif's debt payment scheme.

text.p: Pakistan's foreign reserves rose to $1 billion on Thursday, thanks partly to Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif's appeal for funds to pay off the national debt.
The State (central) Bank of Pakistan (SBP) said in a statement that foreign exchange reserves, excluding bullion, had risen to $1.068 billion from $850 million on February 20.
An SBP official said remittances from Pakistani expatriates had picked up since Sharif made his appeal on Monday, but had no figures on exactly how much had flowed in.

The SBP statement, issued after a board meeting in Lahore, urged all Pakistanis at home and abroad to respond to Sharif's plea for them to give or deposit money in special government accounts to help pay off Pakistan's $30 billion foreign debt.

Bankers said this month's $150 million five-year convertible bond issue by state-run Pakistan Telecommunication Co Ltd and a $115.5 million short-term financing facility arranged by foreign banks for the same company may have contributed to the rise in reserves, which stood at $1.546 billion a year ago.

Sharif launched his plan under the slogan "Qarz Utaro Mulk Sanwaro" (Pay off debt, set country right), tapping a hidden well of patriotism among his countrymen, who have responded with donations ranging from $15 million to a few rupees.
Others are shifting foreign currency into special government bank accounts for a minimum of two years, with or without interest, at the depositor's discretion.
Sharif was showered with money on Wednesday when he paid an impromptu visit to a road construction project near Islamabad.
A six-year-old boy shyly thrust a $5 banknote into the prime minister's hand as traffic came to a halt. Passengers and drivers crowded round and chipped in with their own cash gifts.

The government expects most from an estimated two million Pakistanis working abroad. They have been asked to contribute deposits of at least $1,000 each in return for a personal letter of thanks from the prime minister. Those who send $1 million or more will be invited to receive a medal from Sharif.
Sharif received donations and interest-free deposits totalling two billion rupees from businessmen he invited to a meeting in Islamabad on Wednesday, newspapers reported.
The biggest donation, $15 million, was from Karachi businessman Abu Bakr Sheikhani, a property magnate.
Humbler contributions are flowing in from all sides.
Trade unions and other employees' organisations in the public and private sectors have announced plans to sacrifice one day's earnings or more for Sharif's scheme.
In the armed forces, junior ranks are giving one day's pay and senior ranks two days, while the chiefs of the three armed services are donating one month's salary.
"It's a national cause and I am donating my monthly pocket money," said a student depositing money at one bank where people were queueing up to do the same.
Commerce Minister Ishaq Dar said on Wednesday the government expected to collect $1 billion for its debt repayment fund.
The opposition Pakistan People's Party led by ousted Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto has backed Sharif's idea.

But the religious Jamiat Ulema-i-Islam party led by Maulana Fazlur Rehman, former chairman of a parliamentary foreign affairs committee, says the scheme is an open invitation to drug smugglers to launder their tainted money.
"Now the drug barons will also be awarded national medals," he declared.
The government has promised that no questions will be asked about the source of funds deposited into its accounts.
